labels.value: The OIM taxonomy model should be consistent with the OIM report model, as currently defined. An update to the OIM report model may be considered if it enables a significant improvement to the OIM taxonomy model.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide functionality equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1 constructs that are in common use and consistent with current XBRL best practice. It is not necessary for the OIM taxonomy model to represent every facet within XBRL 2.1's XML syntax.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide label type functionality equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1 constructs that are in common use and consistent with current XBRL best practice. It is not necessary for the OIM taxonomy model to represent every label type within XBRL 2.1's XML syntax.

The OIM taxonomy model has converted label types using a role with a uri identification mechanism to a qname. Labels are defined as a label type. The OIM taxonomy  supports the same set of label types as XBRL 2.1, and supports the ability to define additional label types if necessary. Label types are defined within a an XBRL model and have been expanded to include a datatype attribute, which allows for more precise definition of the content of a label.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide data type functionality equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1, XDT, and other XBRL specifications that are in common use and consistent with current XBRL best practice.

The OIM taxonomy model has converted data type identification from XML Schema type URIs to QNames. Data types are defined as first-class objects within the taxonomy model, enabling the specification of properties such as base types and facets directly within the taxonomy rather than as separate schema artifacts. The full set of XBRL-defined data types (xbrli:*) and XML Schema built-in types (xs:*) are represented as taxonomy objects rather than as external schema definitions, with each type identified by a QName that can be referenced uniformly throughout the model.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide reference type functionality equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1 reference link role types that are in common use and consistent with current XBRL best practice.

The OIM taxonomy model has converted reference types from role URIs to QNames. Reference types are defined as first-class objects within the taxonomy model with properties including allowed objects, replacing the separate link role type registry approach of XBRL 2.1. This enables reference types to be versioned, discovered, and validated within the taxonomy model itself. The OIM taxonomy supports the same set of reference types as XBRL 2.1 and allows additional reference types to be defined within taxonomy extensions.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide property type functionality (formerly known as parts in XBRL 2.1 references and arcrole type properties) equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1 constructs that are in common use and consistent with current XBRL best practice.

The OIM taxonomy model has replaced XBRL 2.1 parts (XML element declarations used in reference types and custom link roles) with property types identified by QNames. Property types are defined as first-class objects within the taxonomy model with properties specifying data types and allowed objects. Unlike XBRL 2.1 where parts required separate XML element declarations in a schema, OIM property types are defined directly within the taxonomy model and identified by QNames, enabling consistent discovery and validation without external schema artifacts.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide relationship type functionality equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1 extended link role types and arcrole types that are in common use and consistent with current XBRL best practice.

The OIM taxonomy model has converted relationship types from extended link role URIs and arcrole URIs to QNames. Relationship types are defined as first-class objects within the taxonomy model with properties including allowed source and target object types, cycle constraints, and network membership. This replaces the separate link role type registry and arcrole type registry approach of XBRL 2.1 with taxonomy-defined objects, enabling processors to discover and validate relationship type constraints directly from the taxonomy model without reference to external registries.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide unit functionality equivalent to that of XBRL 2.1 unit types that are in common use, including support for currency units, physical measurement units, and dimensionless (pure/shares) units.

The OIM taxonomy model has converted unit identification from per-report measure element declarations to QName-identified unit objects defined within importable spec taxonomy modules. The core spec units xbrli:pure and xbrli:shares are defined in the instance spec taxonomy, while the full set of ISO 4217 currency units (iso4217:*) and XBRL Unit Type Registry units (utr:*) are available as separate importable spec taxonomy modules. This replaces the separate Unit Type Registry artifact with taxonomy-defined unit objects, ensuring units have globally consistent QName identifiers and can be discovered and validated as first-class taxonomy objects rather than as entries in an external registry document.

The OIM taxonomy model must be able to provide transform functionality equivalent to that of the iXBRL transform registry, supporting the conversion of human-readable date and numeric formats to XBRL-normalised values in inline XBRL documents.

The OIM taxonomy model has converted iXBRL transforms from URI-identified entries in the iXBRL Transform Registry to QName-identified transform objects defined within an importable spec taxonomy module (xbrltt:*). Transforms are defined as first-class taxonomy objects identified by QNames, replacing the separate iXBRL Transform Registry artifact. This approach enables transforms to be versioned, extended, and referenced uniformly using QNames alongside other taxonomy objects, and allows the set of available transforms to be controlled through the standard taxonomy import mechanism rather than through a separate registry document.
Where the OIM taxonomy model specifies a component as being a collection of items, the model must explicitly state whether the order of those items is semantically significant.
Taxonomy objects should have a globally unique identifier. Object identifiers should be consistent across different object types.

It should be possible to convert existing XBRL 2.1 taxonomies into the OIM taxonomy model, provided that they use functionality within scope of the OIM taxonomy model. Due to the different modelling approaches in use in existing taxonomies, the conversion process may require some configuration in order to define mapping into OIM taxonomy model constructs.

It should be possible for a reporting requirements taxonomy to constrain the ways in which an extension can modify the taxonomy model. Such constraints include: preventing modification or removal of labels or references for existing concepts; preventing the creation of additional labels or references for existing concepts; preventing modification of dimensional structures, such as adding members to a domain. It should be possible to define such constraints at the component level.
It should be possible to efficiently re-use specific components from a large taxonomy.
When importing a taxonomy, it should be possible to control which components of the imported taxonomy are made available to users of the importing taxonomy.

Where a taxonomy imports another taxonomy, it should be possible to determine the nature of the imported components from the import mechanism, so that a processor can avoid or defer loading unnecessary components.
It should be possible to define a taxonomy that provides additional resources for another taxonomy.
Add-on bundles should explicitly identify the taxonomy that they are intended to extend.
It should be possible for a user to augment the taxonomy of a report with compatible add-on bundles.

It should be possible for a hypercube to define any dimension other than the concept core dimension as being required, optional or prohibited (the concept core dimension is required for all facts). These constraints control which facts are included in a hypercube. This extends the functionality in XBRL 2.1 by: allowing taxonomy-defined typed dimensions to be defined as optional; and allowing control over core dimensions.

It should be possible for a hypercube to constrain core dimensions, such as period, units and entity, in addition to taxonomy-defined dimensions. The constraints should include specifying dimensions as required, prohibited or optional for a hypercube. Note that although entity and period must be reported explicitly under XBRL 2.1 syntax, the OIM Report Model treats them as optional. The OIM taxonomy model should be consistent with the OIM report model on this point.
It should be possible to define relationships between fact positions and other taxonomy components.
It should be possible to include facts in a taxonomy. This is intended to support facts that would be common across all reports using a taxonomy, such as a tax rate.
The OIM taxonomy model should support a general-purpose mechanism for defining properties for associating key/value metadata with taxonomy objects.
Property definitions should specify the datatype for corresponding values.
Properties should support list and set-based datatypes.

The model should enable a property definition to specify the categories of objects to which the property may be applied (e.g. concepts, dimensions, domains, relationship types, cubes, or other taxonomy components).

It should be possible for extension taxonomies to define additional properties, or extend the applicability of existing properties, subject to any restrictions imposed by a reporting requirements taxonomy.

The OIM taxonomy model should provide a mechanism for defining structured attributes that may be associated with facts. Attributes allow additional, non-dimensional information to be associated with a fact value.
The OIM taxonomy model should support relationships between taxonomy components.
It should be possible for a taxonomy to define custom relationship types.
The OIM taxonomy model should define relationship types as objects that can be used by the same taxonomy, or re-used in other taxonomies.
A relationship type should define whether the relationship type is hierarchical or non-hierarchical.
A relationship type should define the types of taxonomy components it can relate (e.g., concept-to-concept, domain-to-member, cube-to-dimension, property-to-object).
Relationship types should define whether ordering between relationships of that type is significant.

Calculations should support reconciliation relationships between concepts with different balance types, allowing taxonomy authors to define relationships such as Equity = Assets - Liabilities where the source and target concepts have different balance attributes.
The OIM taxonomy model should support reporting of record-based data. Record-based data is data that consists of repeating sets of facts.
It should be possible to specify the fields that make up a record, and to specify fields as being mandatory within a record, or optional.
It should be possible to specify a field, or set of fields, that must be unique across all reported records.
It should be possible to specify a field, or set of fields, that form a unique identifier (primary key) for a record.
It should be possible to specify a field, or set of fields, that reference the identifier of another record.
Event data is data where each record relates to a specific event. Records will include a mandatory field containing the date and time of the event.
Reference data is data that does not change, or changes very slowly, with the passage of time.
Position data is data that is reported at a point in time.
Listing data is data that that is reported about individual items or units.
Time-series data is data consisting of repeated measurements of a set of data points at a predefined interval.
It should be possible for an OIM taxonomy model to specify certain fact positions as being mandatory, indicating that facts must be reported for those fact positions in a report.
The development of the OIM taxonomy model should yield a roadmap for future development of specifications that provide a coherent set of tabular reporting features.
The OIM taxonomy model may make use of the XML Schema data type system. The OIM taxonomy model must not depend on XML schema complex content models, or other parts of the XML Schema specification.

XBRL adoption has, to a large extent, been driven by regulatory data collection systems. In such a system, a data collection authority publishes a set of reporting requirements that reports submitted to them must comply with. XBRL taxonomies provide a standardised way of communicating these reporting requirements in a structured format. A taxonomy published by, or nominated by, a data collection authority for use by XBRL reports is referred to as a reporting requirements taxonomy. Reporting requirements taxonomies include constraints that reports must adhere to in order to be accepted by the data collection system. XBRL 2.1 taxonomies have limited scope for capturing such constraints in declarative format, and are often accompanied by filing manuals that describe additional filing rules. The OIM taxonomy model should aim to increase the scope of rules that can be captured in a taxonomy, and thus reduce the reliance on separate filing manuals.

CSV is often used to publish large datasets. Using xBRL-CSV for this purpose retains the simplicity of the CSV format whilst providing structured XBRL taxonomy metadata, such as descriptions, translations, links to authoritative definitions, and domain hierarchies. In this use case, there is no reporting requirements taxonomy, as the taxonomy is selected or created by the same entity as the data publisher.

In some filing scenarios, an XBRL report will need to use concepts, dimensions or members that are specific to that entity, and which are therefore not included in the reporting requirements taxonomy. In this case, the report preparer will create an entity-specific report taxonomy that adds the additional definitions. In such an environment the reporting requirements taxonomy is the taxonomy on which the report taxonomy is based. The data collection authority will typically wish to constrain the types of extension permitted in the report taxonomy. For example, the filer may be permitted to add new concepts and labels, but not to modify or remove the labels for existing concepts.

Taxonomies will often import common components from other taxonomies. For example, XBRL International publishes taxonomies containing definitions for the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI), and code lists for ISO currency and country codes. Re-using these definitions prompts consistency between different reporting environments, and reduces effort required to create taxonomies. Similarly, one reporting domain may make use of definitions from another. For example, sustainability reporting may make use of some financial reporting definitions. When building an XBRL taxonomy for such a domain, it is desirable to re-use (rather than redefine) definitions from an authoritative taxonomy, such as the relevant accounting standard taxonomy.
Use case: building a reporting requirements taxonomy

A data collection authority may create a reporting requirements taxonomy by importing other taxonomies. For example, the European Single Electronic Filing (ESEF) system publishes an ESEF reporting requirements taxonomy that imports the IFRS accounting standard taxonomy. This use case is similar to the previous use case; the difference is that in this case, the imported taxonomy provides the vast majority of the reporting definitions, and the reporting requirements taxonomy provides a small number of additional concepts needed by the filing system.
Use case: multi-language taxonomy label resources

Labels for taxonomy definitions are often translated into different languages. A particular user will typically only require labels in a single language. It is desirable to avoid unneeded labels, or to defer loading them until they are requested. This is not currently possible as, under the XBRL 2.1 discovery process, any imported file may import other components of any type.

In some cases, translations of taxonomies are developed by third parties, and may be published after the publication of the underlying taxonomy. Users should be able to easily add additional labels that are released separately from the main taxonomy. XBRL 2.1 does not provide a mechanism for adding additional resources to a taxonomy; the DTS is effectively fixed by the set of taxonomy URLs referenced by the report.

Data quality rules are automated rules that identify potential issues with the data in an XBRL report. Unlike filing rules, a failure of such rules would not generally lead to a rejection of the filing, and the rules may be maintained by a third party. It should be possible for users to selectively apply such additional rules, in order to test for conformance with data quality rules. In XBRL 2.1, XBRL Formula rules form part of the DTS, which is effectively fixed by the set of taxonomy URLs referenced by the report. As such there is no standard way to augment the DTS with additional rules.

A common scenario in financial reporting is to disclose a figure that is the total for a particular breakdown, and also disclose that the total amount is attributable to a component of that breakdown. This is often done implicitly by omitting a separate figure for the total. This creates a challenge for XBRL reporting, as tagging the figure as either the total or the component risks losing information. Allowing relationships to be associated with fact positions would allow the definition of a relationship to associate the fact position with the domain member representing the specific component to capture this information.

In financial reporting it is common to express a relationship between concepts with different balance types via a reconciliation, for example Equity (credit) = (+1) Assets (debit) – (–1) Liabilities (credit). In XBRL 2.1, the summation-item arc role does not accommodate this directly because the balance-type consistency rules prevent mixing credit and debit concepts in the same summation. A dedicated reconciliation flag on the summation-item relationship allows taxonomy authors to explicitly declare such cross-balance reconciliations, enabling processors to validate them consistently.

The OIM taxonomy model MUST support a date range data type for use with typed dimensions, where a range is expressed as an integer number of days combined with an optional open-ended marker. A value consists of either: (a) an exact non-negative integer number of days representing the upper bound of a bounded bucket (e.g. 30 for a 0–30 day bucket, 60 for a 31–60 day bucket); or (b) a designated sentinel value indicating an open-ended or unbounded range (e.g. representing 'thereafter' or 'not applicable'). Taxonomy authors SHOULD define the set of standard bucket boundaries applicable to their domain. Because different reporting regimes use different bucket boundaries (for example, maturity ladders may differ between banking and insurance), the type itself does not mandate specific breakpoints, but enables applications to recognise and compare values that share the same bucket structure across reporters.

The OIM taxonomy model MUST support a semi-open coded data type for use with typed dimensions. This type is a string type where a taxonomy may define a recommended set of standard values (a code list), while still permitting reporters to supply values outside that set. Applications SHOULD use the defined code list to guide reporters towards consistent use of standard values and to flag non-standard values for review, but MUST NOT treat non-standard values as invalid. This prevents fragmentation where different reporters coin different string literals for the same concept, while retaining the flexibility needed to handle genuinely novel or not-applicable values.

The OIM taxonomy model MUST support a partial date data type that allows a date value to be expressed at varying levels of temporal precision: year only (YYYY), year and month (YYYY-MM), full date (YYYY-MM-DD), date with hour (YYYY-MM-DDTHH), date with hour and minute (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM), or full date-time (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS). This is required because some reported data is only known to a certain level of precision, for example an investment schedule where the maturity month and year of a bond are known but the exact day is not.
Use case: date range typed dimension

Regulatory reporting commonly requires data to be broken down by time-to-maturity or ageing buckets, such as 0–30 days, 31–60 days, 61–90 days, and thereafter. These buckets are used, for example, in liquidity coverage ratio reporting, maturity ladder schedules, and trade ageing reports. The challenge is that different regulators and even different reporting templates within the same organisation use different bucket boundaries, and the final bucket is always open-ended (representing any duration beyond the last defined boundary). Under the current XBRL typed dimension model there is no way to represent this pattern in a way that is comparable across reporters: a string-only dimension allows inconsistent free-text, while a pure integer dimension cannot represent the open-ended 'thereafter' bucket. A date range data type solves this by combining a non-negative integer (number of days representing the upper bound of each bucket) with a designated sentinel for the open-ended bucket, allowing applications to identify matching bucket structures across reporters and to compare data that uses the same breakpoints while still accommodating schemas that differ in their choice of bucket boundaries.
Use case: semi-open coded typed dimension

In many regulatory and financial reporting contexts, typed dimensions categorise facts by a characteristic that has a recognised set of standard values, but where reporters may legitimately need to use values outside that set. For example, a 'Product Type' typed dimension may have standard values such as 'Bond', 'Equity' and 'Derivative', which should be used consistently by all reporters so that data can be aggregated and compared across submissions. However, a reporter may encounter an instrument that does not fit any standard category, or where the product type is unknown or not applicable, requiring a free-form string value. Under the current XBRL model, there is no mechanism for a taxonomy to define a recommended set of values for a typed dimension; applications cannot distinguish a recognised coded value from an arbitrary free-form string. A semi-open coded data type addresses this by allowing the taxonomy to publish a code list of recommended values while still permitting non-standard values, enabling applications to guide reporters towards consistent codes, to warn when a non-standard value is used, and to support data comparison and aggregation across different reporters.

Financial institutions and regulators frequently encounter data where the exact date of a transaction or contract event is not known with full precision. A common example is an investment schedule reporting the maturity dates of fixed-income instruments: the maturity year and month may be known from summary records, but not the exact day. Similarly, certain regulatory filings require reporting of the vintage year of an asset, or the quarter in which a contractual milestone occurs. In all these cases, reporting a fabricated full date (e.g. setting the day to the first of the month) misrepresents the precision of the data and introduces errors in downstream analysis. The xbrli:partialDate data type addresses this by allowing a value to be expressed at whichever level of temporal precision is actually known, from year only through to full date-time, in alignment with ISO 8601 truncated date representations.

The OIM taxonomy model implements the semi-open coded type requirement (REQ-DT002) through the openEnumeration property on the dataType object. Rather than defining a separate runtime data type, the taxonomy author defines a standard data type (typically derived from xs:string or xs:token) and sets openEnumeration to true to signal that the enumeration list is a recommended code list rather than a closed constraint. When openEnumeration is false (the default), only values in the enumeration array are valid. When true, values outside the defined enumeration are permitted but applications SHOULD treat them as non-standard and MAY flag them for review. This moves the semi-open coded type concept from a registry or annotation convention into a first-class property of the taxonomy-defined dataType object, identified by QName, enabling consistent tooling support and validation behaviour across processors without a separate artifact.

The partial date data type is implemented as a standard data type within the OIM taxonomy model, with a defined  data type. This allows taxonomy authors to use the partial date type in their taxonomies without needing to define it themselves. The datatype can only be used with concept objects, and is not available for use with typed dimensions.

The ordering requirement (REQ-GEN003) is implemented through two mechanisms. First, all arrays of objects or values in the taxonomy model indicate explicitly whether they are ordered or unordered, ensuring processors know when sequence is significant. Second, for relationships specifically, the base specification defines the xbrl:order property on xbrl:relationshipObject, allowing taxonomy authors to assign an explicit numeric ordering to relationships within a network. Where xbrl:order is present, processors MUST present or process the relationships in ascending order of that value. Where xbrl:order is absent, the ordering of relationships is undefined and processors SHOULD NOT infer significance from document order.

The object identifier requirement (REQ-GEN004) is implemented by identifying all referenceable objects in the taxonomy model by a QName rather than by URI or local ID. Every named model object — concepts, dimensions, cubes, networks, members, data types, label types, relationship types, and others — carries a name property whose value is a QName. This means object identity is never tied to a file path, schema location, or fragment identifier; no URI or ID attribute is required to reference an object from another part of the taxonomy. Where the OIM JSON serialisation format needs to resolve a QName prefix to a namespace URI, a mapping from prefix to namespace URI is provided in the documentInfo section of the instance or taxonomy document. This separation of logical identity (QName) from physical location (file or URI) allows taxonomies to be refactored, relocated, or selectively imported without breaking cross-references, and processors can resolve any object reference without knowledge of the file structure.

The OIM Report Model compatibility requirement (REQ-GEN001) is implemented by designing the OIM taxonomy model around the same set of core dimensions used by the OIM Report Model: xbrl:concept, xbrl:period, xbrl:entity, xbrl:unit, and xbrl:language. Facts in an OIM taxonomy model fact space are identified by exactly these dimensions, ensuring that facts from a taxonomy and facts from an instance report share a common addressing scheme. Processors can therefore treat taxonomy-supplied facts and report facts uniformly, enabling consistent evaluation of calculation and dimensional constraints across both sources.

The backwards compatibility requirement (REQ-GEN005) is addressed through a dedicated XBRL 2.1 XML conversion pipeline in the reference implementation. The xbrl-parser.js module parses XBRL 2.1 instance documents and converts them to OIM report model facts, mapping contexts to xbrl:period and xbrl:entity dimensions, units to xbrl:unit, and concepts to xbrl:concept. Duration contexts are represented as ISO 8601 intervals (startDate/endDate), and nil facts are represented with the xbrl:nil property. The XBRL 2.1 taxonomy converter maps linkbases, arcrole types, role types, and schema elements to corresponding OIM taxonomy model objects. Configuration is provided via a factMap (xbrl:XBRL21XML) that controls the mapping behaviour.

The restrict-extension requirement (REQ-EXT001) is implemented through the finalTaxonomy property on an xbrlModel object. When finalTaxonomy is set to true, extension taxonomies are prohibited from modifying the objects defined in that taxonomy. This includes preventing addition, removal, or modification of labels, references, or dimensional structure. Taxonomy authors can thus mark specific modules as sealed against extension, while leaving other modules open. The restriction is enforced at the taxonomy model level, providing a declarative alternative to filing manual instructions about what extension activity is permitted.

The efficient reuse requirement (REQ-EXT002) is implemented through the importedTaxonomies array on an xbrlModel object. Each entry specifies an xbrlModelName identifying the taxonomy to import, and an optional importObjectTypes array that filters which categories of objects are imported. By specifying importObjectTypes, a taxonomy author can import only the concepts, labels, cubes, or relationships needed, avoiding the overhead of loading the entire source taxonomy. This replaces the XBRL 2.1 approach where any imported schema or linkbase brought in all of its content regardless of the importing taxonomy's needs.

The export control requirement (REQ-EXT003) is implemented through the importObjectTypes filter and the optional selectionExpression property on an importedTaxonomy entry. The importing taxonomy author specifies which categories of objects from the imported taxonomy are made available in the resulting compiled taxonomy. Additionally, the selectionExpression allows a subset of objects within a category to be selected using a query expression. Objects excluded by these filters are not visible to downstream users of the importing taxonomy, enabling a taxonomy builder to expose only the relevant subset of a large shared taxonomy.

The import identification requirement (REQ-EXT004) is implemented through the modelForm property on an xbrlModel object, where a value of 'module' indicates that the taxonomy is a loadable component providing a self-contained set of definitions. Processors can inspect the modelForm value in an import entry to determine the nature of the imported content before loading it. Combined with importObjectTypes, this allows a processor to defer or skip loading taxonomy modules that do not contain the required object types, enabling selective loading strategies for large taxonomies with many modules.

The extension bundle requirement (REQ-EXT005) is implemented through the modelForm value 'addOnBundle' on an xbrlModel object. An add-on bundle is a taxonomy module that provides additional resources (such as labels or validation rules) for another taxonomy, without modifying the objects defined there. Processors can recognise add-on bundles by their modelForm, and users can selectively merge compatible bundles with a base taxonomy. This enables third-party translations, data quality rule sets, and other optional accessories to be packaged and applied to a taxonomy independently of the taxonomy publisher.

The extend target identification requirement (REQ-EXT006) is implemented through the extendTargetName property on an importedTaxonomy entry within an add-on bundle. The extendTargetName identifies the xbrlModel that the bundle is intended to augment. Processors can use this value to verify that a bundle is compatible with the base taxonomy before merging it, and can surface the intended target to users selecting which bundles to apply. This provides an explicit, machine-readable declaration of the relationship between an add-on bundle and its target taxonomy.

The taxonomy composition requirement (REQ-EXT007) is implemented through the ability to include multiple importedTaxonomies entries in a compiled or module-form xbrlModel, where one or more of the imported entries are add-on bundles identified by modelForm: 'addOnBundle'. A user augments the base taxonomy by adding bundle entries to the importedTaxonomies list. The processor merges the resources from each bundle into the compiled model according to the bundle's extendTargetName, enabling a user to compose a personalised taxonomy from a common base plus optional add-ons without modifying the base taxonomy itself.

The hypercube dimension constraint requirement (REQ-DIM001) is implemented through the allowDomainFacts property on a cubeDimension object. When allowDomainFacts is true, facts with the dimension value set to a domain member (rather than a leaf member only) are included in the hypercube, implementing the 'optional' constraint. When false (the default), only leaf member values are matched. For core dimensions such as xbrl:unit and xbrl:language, the required/optional/prohibited constraint is represented by including or omitting the dimension from the cubeDimension list, or by setting a dedicated constraint property. This provides fine-grained per-dimension control over which facts are included in each hypercube.

The core dimension constraint requirement (REQ-DIM002) is implemented by allowing cubeDimension entries to specify any of the standard core dimension names: xbrl:concept, xbrl:period, xbrl:entity, xbrl:unit, and xbrl:language. A cube author can include xbrl:unit as a cubeDimension with a required constraint to mandate that all facts in the cube carry a unit, or include xbrl:language as optional to permit multilingual fact sets. The OIM taxonomy model follows the OIM report model in treating period and entity as optional, so a cube that does not include xbrl:period in its cubeDimensions does not require facts to carry a period value.

The fact position relationship requirement (REQ-FP001) is implemented by allowing facts to appear as source or target endpoints in relationship networks. A fact position can be identified by its set of dimension values and included as a node in a network via the relationships array. This enables taxonomy authors to define relationships such as xbrl:fact-footnote (linking a fact position to an explanatory fact) or xbrl:fact-explanatoryFact, as well as custom relationship types that link specific dimensional positions to domain members representing components of an aggregate.

The taxonomy-supplied facts requirement (REQ-TF001) is implemented through the facts array on an xbrlModel object. Each element of the facts array is a fact object with the same structure as instance report facts, identified by factDimensions and carrying a value. Taxonomy facts are loaded as part of the taxonomy model and are available to processors evaluating constraints, calculations, or queries that span both instance and taxonomy-supplied values. This allows, for example, a statutory tax rate to be defined in the taxonomy and referenced in calculation consistency checks rather than being supplied in every individual report.

The property model requirement (REQ-PROP001) is implemented through a properties array that may appear on any taxonomy object. Each entry in the array is an object with a property key (a QName identifying the property type) and a value. This uniform key/value metadata mechanism is available on concepts, dimensions, cubes, networks, relationship types, label types, reference types, and other first-class model objects. The property mechanism replaces the ad-hoc use of custom XML attributes or separate linkbase entries that was required for per-object metadata in XBRL 2.1.

The property type requirement (REQ-PROP002) is implemented through propertyType objects defined in the taxonomy model. Each propertyType object carries a name (QName), a dataType specifying the expected value type, and optional allowedObjects and cardinality constraints. Processors use the dataType to validate property values and to determine appropriate rendering. By defining property types as first-class taxonomy objects, the model enables tools to discover available properties, validate their values, and generate appropriate input controls, replacing the implicit type-by-convention approach of XBRL 2.1 custom attributes.

The collection type requirement (REQ-PROP003) is implemented by supporting the dataType value xbrli:collection on propertyType objects, combined with a collectionType property that specifies the item type and whether the collection is ordered (list) or unordered (set). Processors treat properties of collection type as arrays of values. This enables property types such as xbrl:excludedIntervals (a set of interval values) or custom multi-value metadata to be defined within the taxonomy model with well-specified cardinality and item type constraints.

The property applicability requirement (REQ-PROP004) is implemented through the allowedObjects array on propertyType objects. Each entry names a domain class (e.g. xbrl:conceptObject, xbrl:dimensionObject, xbrl:cubeObject) to which the property may be applied. Processors can use this constraint to validate that a property is not applied to an unsupported object type, and tools can use it to surface only relevant properties when editing a particular object. This replaces the implicit applicability rules encoded in XBRL 2.1 linkbase schemas with an explicit, discoverable declaration in the taxonomy model.

The property extensibility requirement (REQ-PROP005) is implemented by allowing extension taxonomy modules to define additional propertyType objects using their own namespace prefixes, and by allowing extension taxonomies to include properties using those types on objects they or the base taxonomy define. Extension-defined property types are identified by QName, so that they can be unambiguously distinguished from base taxonomy properties. If the base taxonomy's finalTaxonomy flag is set, the extension may not add properties to base taxonomy objects, but may freely define and use properties on its own objects.

The fact attributes requirement (REQ-ATT001) is implemented through the properties array on fact objects in the OIM instance model. Each element of the properties array carries a property QName and a value, enabling non-dimensional metadata such as xbrl:nil (indicating a nil fact), xbrl:reportAttribute (statistical status or audit information), or custom fact-level annotations to be attached to individual fact values. The properties are defined by propertyType objects in the taxonomy with allowedObjects including xbrl:factObject, ensuring that property types are validated and discoverable. This replaces the ad-hoc use of footnote links and custom XML attributes for fact-level metadata in XBRL 2.1.

The relationships requirement (REQ-REL001) is implemented through the networks array on an xbrlModel object. Each network carries a name (QName), a relationshipTypeName identifying the type of relationships it contains, an optional roots array, and a relationships array. Each relationship entry has source and target QNames identifying the connected objects, and an optional order property. Processors can discover all relationships between named taxonomy objects by iterating the networks array, providing a uniform structure regardless of the relationship type or the object types connected.

The custom relationship types requirement (REQ-RT001) is implemented through the relationshipTypes array on an xbrlModel object. Each relationshipType object carries a name (QName) identifying it for use as the relationshipTypeName in a network, and optional uri, cycles, sourceObjects, targetObjects, and ordered properties. Extension taxonomies can add new relationship type objects in their own namespace. Processors look up the relationship type name in the merged model to determine the applicable constraints when validating or processing a network.

The built-in relationship type requirement (REQ-RT002) is addressed by the OIM base specification defining a complete set of standard relationship types identified by xbrl: prefixed QNames. These include xbrl:parent-child (presentation hierarchy), xbrl:summation-item (calculation), xbrl:fact-footnote, xbrl:fact-explanatoryFact, domain-member relationships, and others corresponding to the arc roles defined in XBRL 2.1. Each is defined as a relationshipType object in the base spec taxonomy module, making them discoverable and reusable in any taxonomy that imports the base spec.

The hierarchical relationship type requirement (REQ-RT003) is implemented through the cycles property on a relationshipType object. When cycles is 'none', the relationship type forms a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and is considered hierarchical; processors must reject any network that contains a cycle. When cycles is 'undirected', undirected cycles are also forbidden, forming a tree. When cycles is 'any', cycles are permitted and the relationship type is non-hierarchical. This provides a declarative, per-type control over cycle constraints, replacing the implicit hierarchical/non-hierarchical distinction encoded in XBRL 2.1 arcrole URIs.

The relationship applicability requirement (REQ-RT004) is implemented through the sourceObjects and targetObjects arrays on a relationshipType object. Each entry names a domain class (e.g. xbrl:conceptObject, xbrl:memberObject) that is a permitted source or target for relationships of that type. Processors validate that relationships in a network conform to the declared source/target constraints. This replaces the implicit object-type applicability rules encoded in XBRL 2.1 arcrole URIs and linkbase schemas with an explicit, discoverable declaration in the taxonomy model.

The relationship ordering requirement (REQ-RT005) is implemented through the order property on individual relationship objects within a network, combined with the ordered property (boolean) on the relationshipType object indicating whether the type supports ordering. Processors sort relationships with an order value in ascending numeric order and present them before any unordered relationships. When no order values are present and the type is not ordered, document order is not considered significant. This replaces the implicit ordering semantics of XBRL 2.1 presentation arcs, where the order attribute was always numeric and mandatory.

The calculation reconciliation requirement (REQ-RT006) is implemented through the xbrl:reconciliation property on xbrl:summation-item relationship objects. When xbrl:reconciliation is true, the normal balance-consistency rule is inverted: a weight of 1 requires the source and target concepts to have different xbrla:balance values, and a weight of -1 requires them to have the same xbrla:balance value. This allows the definition of equity-style reconciliations of the form Total (credit) = (+1) Component (debit) + (–1) Contra (credit). When xbrl:reconciliation is false or absent, the standard rules apply: weight 1 requires the same balance and weight -1 requires different balances. The property is optional and defaults to false.

The record-based data reporting requirement (REQ-NFR001) is implemented through the cube and cubeDimension model objects. A cube represents a repeating record structure with a defined set of fields (cubeDimensions). Each fact that falls within the cube's scope provides a value for one field of one record. The set of dimension values common to all facts in a record identifies the record instance, and the xbrl:concept dimension identifies the field within that record. By defining all fields as cubeDimensions with appropriate required/optional constraints, a taxonomy author fully specifies the structure of the repeating record.

The mandatory record fields requirement (REQ-NFR002) is implemented through the allowDomainFacts property and the presence of a cubeDimension entry for each field. A dimension included in the cubeDimensions list is considered required for facts in that cube by default (allowDomainFacts: false). Optional fields are indicated by allowDomainFacts set to true or by an explicit optional constraint marker on the cubeDimension. This allows a taxonomy author to specify, for each field of a record, whether it must always be reported or may be omitted.

The unique record fields requirement (REQ-NFR003) is addressed through the fact space uniqueness guarantee provided by the cube model. Because a cube's fact space is defined as the Cartesian product of its cubeDimension value sets, each combination of dimension values can hold at most one fact per xbrl:concept. Taxonomy authors define unique constraints by specifying the set of cubeDimensions whose combined values must be unique across records. Processor validation checks that no two facts in the cube share the same dimension value combination for the specified unique-constraint dimensions.

The primary key requirement (REQ-NFR004) is implemented through a dedicated primaryKey property on a cube object. The value is a list of dimension QNames whose combined values form the unique identifier for a record. Processors validate that no two records in the fact space share the same primary key values. The primary key declaration also enables cross-cube foreign key references to be validated without ambiguity.

The foreign key requirement (REQ-NFR005) is implemented through a foreignKey property on a cube or cubeDimension object. A foreign key entry specifies the source dimension(s) whose value(s) must match the primary key of a target cube. Processors validate referential integrity by checking that every foreign key value in the reporting fact space corresponds to a record in the referenced cube. This enables relational-style cross-record validation within the OIM taxonomy model without the need for a separate XBRL Formula rule.

The event data requirement (REQ-NFR006) is implemented by including the xbrl:period dimension as a required cubeDimension with an instant period type constraint on the cube. Each record in an event-data cube carries a mandatory timestamp in the xbrl:period dimension, identifying the date and time of the event. Additional event metadata fields are defined as other cubeDimensions. This uses the existing core dimension mechanism rather than requiring a separate event-timestamp field type, maintaining consistency with the OIM report model's treatment of period as a core dimension.

The reference data requirement (REQ-NFR007) is addressed by defining reference data tables as cubes with the xbrl:period dimension either absent (period-independent) or constrained to instant values. Reference data cubes represent slowly changing or static look-up tables. The taxonomy author marks a cube as reference data by setting a xbrl:referenceData property on the cube object, enabling processors and user interfaces to identify and treat these cubes differently from transactional data cubes.

The position data requirement (REQ-NFR010) is implemented by defining position data cubes with the xbrl:period dimension constrained to instant-type periods. Each record in a position-data cube represents the state of an item at a specific point in time. Model authors set the period type to 'instant' on the relevant cubeDimension, enabling processors to validate that all facts in the cube carry an instant period value rather than a duration period.

The listing data requirement (REQ-NFR011) is implemented by defining listing data cubes where each record represents an individual item or unit, identified by a unique key in one or more cubeDimensions. The xbrl:period dimension may be absent (period-independent) or constrained as appropriate. Model authors set a xbrl:listingData property on the cube object to signal that the cube follows the listing data pattern, distinguishing it from aggregated financial statement data.

The time-series data requirement (REQ-NFR012) is implemented through the xbrl:timeSeriesType, xbrl:intervalOfMeasurement, and xbrl:intervalConvention property types on cube and concept objects. A time-series cube constrains the xbrl:period dimension to duration periods of a fixed interval length, so that a sequence of period values forms a uniform time series. The xbrl:intervalOfMeasurement property declares the interval duration (e.g. P1M for monthly), and xbrl:intervalConvention records whether intervals are measured from period start or end. Together these properties enable processors to align, resample, and aggregate time-series data correctly.

The mandatory elements requirement (REQ-RC001) is implemented through the requiredCubes property on an xbrlModel or cube object. A requiredCubes entry specifies a cube (by QName) and optionally a minimum cardinality, indicating that reports using the model must include at least that many facts satisfying the cube's constraints. Processors evaluate mandatory element compliance by checking that the reporting instance contains the required facts for each entry in requiredCubes. This provides a declarative, model-defined mandatory reporting requirement as an alternative to XBRL Formula assertions.

The tabular reporting requirement (REQ-TAB001) is addressed through the tableTemplates, factMaps, and factSources constructs in the OIM  model. A tableTemplate defines a two-dimensional rendering of a cube including row and column headers and cell bindings. A factMap specifies how facts are extracted from or written to an external format such as xBRL-CSV. A factSource combines tableTemplate and factMap declarations to define a complete reporting template (form). Together these constructs provide the roadmap for coherent tabular reporting functionality across xBRL-CSV, inline XBRL table rendering, and other tabular representations.

The XML Schema technical requirement (REQ-TECH001) is implemented by representing all XML Schema built-in data types (xs:string, xs:decimal, xs:date, xs:boolean, etc.) as first-class dataType objects in the OIM base spec model, identified by their QNames. The OIM  model uses these QNames as baseType references when defining XBRL data types, making the XSD type system available to the model without requiring processors to load an XML Schema processor or to evaluate XSD complex content models. XBRL-defined types (xbrli:*) similarly derive from these xs: base types via the baseType chain, providing the full XBRL type system through simple QName lookups.

The date range type requirement (REQ-DT003) is implemented through the xbrli:dateRange built-in data type in the OIM  model. A dateRange value represents either an exact non-negative integer number of days (representing the upper inclusive bound of a bucket, e.g. 30 for a 0–30 day bucket) or the sentinel string 'unbounded' representing an open-ended 'thereafter' bucket. The type is defined as derived from xs:string with a pattern facet, and is intended for use with typed dimensions defining maturity ladder or ageing bucket breakdowns. The xbrli:dateRange type is available for import via the xbrli spec module and can be used by model authors without defining a custom data type.
